artificial-intelligence: AI and machine learning as a subject: LLMs, neural networks, embeddings (e.g. word2vec), model training and architecture, prompt engineering, RAG, AI tooling and applied ML. Covers both conceptual explainers and practical AI/ML usage. Not general CS theory (that goes to computer-science) unless the link is specifically about AI/ML.
audio: Audio as a subject: audio engineering, sound design, music production, audio formats and codecs, DSP, hardware, and audio software. The topic is sound itself, not the platform it runs on.
computer-network: Computer networking: protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP, DNS, etc.), network architecture, routing, packets, sockets, CDNs, and networking concepts. Qualified as 'computer-' because a bare 'network' would be ambiguous at the top level.
computer-science: Computer science fundamentals and theory that are language- and platform-agnostic: algorithms and data structures, computation, how computers work (CPUs, memory), CS curricula and learning paths (CS50, nand2tetris, teachyourselfcs, roadmaps), debugging as a general skill, reading CS papers. Concepts, not how-to-code-in-X (that goes to programming-languages) and not AI-specific (that goes to artificial-intelligence).
computer-security: Information and computer security: cryptography (ciphers, key exchange, crypto fundamentals like crypto101 and Diffie-Hellman), application/web security, authentication, vulnerabilities, threat models, and security practices. Qualified as 'computer-' so it isn't confused with physical security or financial securities. Not cryptocurrency.
cryptocurrency: Cryptocurrency and blockchain as a subject: coins and tokens, blockchain technology, DeFi, wallets, smart contracts, and crypto markets. Distinct from computer-security (cryptography) and finance (traditional finance).
databases: Databases as a cross-cutting concern: relational and NoSQL systems, query languages (SQL), data modeling, indexing, transactions, ORMs, and database internals. Top-level because databases span server, mobile, and analytics contexts rather than being strictly server-side.
design: Visual and experience design: UI design, UX, interaction and visual design, typography, color, layout, and design systems/tooling from a visual standpoint. NOT system or API design (that is server/architecture) — this tag is strictly about how things look and feel.
devops: DevOps and operations: CI/CD, infrastructure-as-code and infrastructure-from-code, containers and orchestration, deployment, monitoring/observability, cloud operations, and the practices around running software in production.
editors: Code editors and IDEs as a subject. Holds directly any general editor content (editor comparisons, cross-editor concepts like LSP from the editor side); children narrow to a specific editor. Distinct from `terminal` — covers both terminal-based and GUI editors.
editors/neovim: Neovim specifically: nvim configuration, plugins, LSP setup, Lua config for nvim, and Neovim-focused workflows.
editors/zed: The Zed editor specifically: Zed configuration, keybindings, vim mode in Zed, AI features, migration from other editors, and Zed-specific workflows.
finance: Traditional/personal finance as a subject: investing, markets, money management, economics, accounting. Distinct from cryptocurrency and from marketing/analytics (business metrics).
marketing: Marketing, growth, and discoverability as a concern. Holds directly any general marketing/growth content (ads, content marketing, email, positioning) that doesn't fit a child. Children narrow to specific measurement/discoverability areas.
marketing/analytics: Product and web analytics: tracking, metrics, dashboards, instrumentation, A/B testing, and measuring user behavior across platforms.
marketing/seo: Search engine optimization: on-page and technical SEO, search ranking, discoverability via search engines, and search-driven growth.
math: Mathematics as a subject: arithmetic through advanced topics, math concepts and references. Pure math content; applied math that is really about a CS or security topic should go to that tag instead.
mobile: Mobile as a platform. Holds directly any mobile-platform content (iOS/Android concepts, mobile UX, app store topics) that doesn't fit a child. Children narrow to specific aspects of mobile work.
mobile/development: Building mobile apps: mobile dev concepts, tooling, SDKs, and platform-specific development not tied to a single framework. Holds general mobile-dev links directly; framework-specific content goes to children.
mobile/development/react-native: React Native specifically: RN framework, components, navigation, native modules, and the RN ecosystem.
operating-systems: Operating systems as a platform/environment. Holds directly any general OS-level content; children narrow to a specific OS. (Parent kept to accommodate adding linux/windows later.)
operating-systems/macos: macOS environment: system setup and configuration, window managers (e.g. yabai), package managers used on macOS (Homebrew, Nix), macOS-specific commands and defaults, and Mac power-user tooling.
programming-languages: Programming languages and language-level topics. Holds directly any language-specific content for a language without its own child (e.g. Go, Python, Zig), plus general 'learning a language' material and language/paradigm comparisons. Children are individual languages with enough content to stand alone.
programming-languages/c: The C language: syntax, memory management, pointers, and C-specific learning resources and projects.
programming-languages/javascript: JavaScript and its runtime/toolchain ecosystem (including runtimes like Node/Bun internals viewed from the JS side, bundlers, and JS language features). TypeScript has its own tag.
programming-languages/lua: The Lua language: syntax, embedding, and Lua-specific content (often overlaps with Neovim config, but pure-language material lives here).
programming-languages/rust: The Rust language: ownership/borrowing, the type system, cargo/crates, and Rust-specific learning and projects.
programming-languages/typescript: TypeScript specifically: the type system, tsconfig, type-level programming, and TS-specific tooling and patterns.
science: Natural and general science (non-computer): physics, biology, chemistry, astronomy, etc. Explicitly distinct from computer-science, which holds CS theory.
server: Server-side / backend as a concern. Holds directly any backend content that doesn't fit a child. Children narrow to architecture vs. hands-on development.
server/architecture: Backend and system architecture: API design (REST, OpenAPI, Google AIPs, pagination, contract testing), distributed systems, microservices, messaging (RabbitMQ, Pub/Sub), event-driven architecture, and high-level system design. The 'design of systems', as opposed to visual design.
server/development: Hands-on backend development: building servers and services, frameworks, runtime concerns, and server-side implementation. Holds general backend-dev links directly; specific runtimes go to children.
server/development/node: Node.js specifically: the Node runtime, its APIs, ecosystem, and Node-based server development.
tech-culture: Tech industry and developer culture: commentary, history, people and companies, career and ways-of-working, opinion essays, and the social/cultural side of software. Not how-to or reference material — that belongs in a topic tag. Distinct from blogs (a source type) — tech-culture is about subject matter.
terminal: The terminal and command-line environment, OS-agnostic. Holds directly any general terminal/CLI content (terminal emulators like Ghostty, SSH, general CLI workflow) that doesn't fit a child.
terminal/dotfiles: Dotfiles and the configuration/ricing community: shared dotfiles repos, system and shell configuration setups, and config inspiration. Broader than just Neovim — covers whole-environment dotfiles.
terminal/shell: Shells and shell usage: bash/zsh/fish, shell scripting, shell configuration, SSH, and understanding how shells work.
terminal/tooling: Command-line tools and utilities: CLI programs, terminal productivity tools, and tooling that lives in the terminal but isn't a shell, editor, or dotfiles setup.
vcs: Version control as a concern. Holds directly any general version-control content; children narrow to a specific system. (Parent kept to accommodate non-git VCS later.)
vcs/git: Git specifically: git commands and workflows, branching strategies, git internals, and Git hosting/collaboration.
web: The web as a platform (primarily client-side). Holds directly any general web content that doesn't fit a child. Children narrow to specific web concerns. Server-side web work lives under 'server'.
web/accessibility: Web accessibility: a11y standards (WCAG, ARIA), inclusive design, assistive technology, and accessible front-end implementation.
web/development: Front-end / client-side web development: HTML, JavaScript in the browser, frameworks, browser APIs, performance, and general web app implementation. The catch-all for web building that isn't specifically styling or accessibility.
web/styling: Web styling and presentation: CSS, layout techniques, design tokens, styling frameworks and methodologies, animations, and the visual implementation layer of the web.
blogs: Blogs and personal sites worth following as sources: individual writers' sites, company engineering blogs, and ongoing publications. A source-type tag (where it comes from) rather than a subject tag (what it's about) — a post may also carry a topic tag.
